Abstract
The artificial intelligence era has witnessed a surge of demand in detection and
recognition of biometric information, with applications from financial services
to information security. However, the physical separation of sensing, memory,
and computational units in traditional biometric systems introduces severe
decision latency and operational power consumption. Herein, an in-sensor res-
ervoir computing (RC) system based on MoTe2/BaTiO3 optical synapses is pro-
posed to detect and recognize the faces and fingerprints information. In optical
operation mode, the device exhibits low energy consumption of 41.2 pJ, long
retention time of 3  104 s, high endurance of 104 switching cycles, and
multifunctional sensing-memory-computing visual simulations. The light
intensity-dependent optical sensing and multilevel optical storage properties
are exploited to achieve sunburned eye simulation and image memory func-
tions. These nonlinear, multi-state, short-term storage, and long-term memory
characteristics make MoTe2/BaTiO3 optical synapses a suitable reservoir layer
and readout layer, with short-term properties to project complicated input fea-
tures into high-dimensional output features, and long-term properties to be
used as a readout layer, thus further building an in-sensor RC system for face
and fingerprint recognition. Under the 40% Gaussian noise environment, the
system achieves 91.73% recognition accuracy for face and 97.50% for finger-
print images, and experimental verification is carried out, which shows poten-
tial in practical applications. These results provide a strategy for constructing a
high-performance
in-sensor
RC
system
for
high-accuracy
biometric
identification.

INTRODUCTION
Face and fingerprint recognition are essential technolo-
gies in biometrics for analyzing and authenticating user
identity features.1–4 They are playing an increasingly crit-
ical role in financial services, communications, informa-
tion security, and other fields.5–8 With the booming
development of artificial intelligence technology, the
demand for detection and recognition of biometric infor-
mation including face and fingerprint has exploded.9–11
However, the traditional face and fingerprint recognition
systems have physically separated sensing, memory, and
processing units, which leads to operational delays,
increases operational complexity, and inevitably reduces
system energy efficiency.11–14 Therefore, in order to
reduce the amount of redundant information generated
during the computation process and increase the compu-
tational power of the recognition system, there is an
urgent need to develop an innovative photoelectric device
and processing architecture.
Inspired by the human sensory system, the in-
memory computing architecture based on visual sensors
drastically improves the efficiency of face and fingerprint
recognition, owing to the opportunity to not only mimic
the human retina for sensing, storing, and preprocessing
optical information within a single device, but also to
take advantage of parallel computation in artificial neural
network (ANN).15–19 Among the various frameworks of
ANNs, reservoir computing (RC) can nonlinearly project
complicated input signals into high-dimensional spaces
for recognition, so that spatio-temporal information can
be computed simply and quickly at low computational
cost.20–23
RC-based
systems
have
demonstrated
the
energy efficiency of learning, providing a potential solu-
tion for implementation of processing spatio-temporal
pattern classification, recognition, and prediction.24,25
However, these applications are usually performed in
electrical operation mode, which requires additional sen-
sors and auxiliary circuit design, and its readout layer still
relies on von Neumann architecture, thus increasing the
computational delay and redundant data. The in-sensor
RC system based on photoelectric devices is capable of
sensing and responding to external light stimuli, enabling
sensory information computation.26,27
Importantly,
realizing
in-sensor
RC
computing
requires photoelectric devices with nonlinear dynamic
characteristics, short-term storage, and long-term synaptic
properties. Recently, 2D semiconducting materials with
rich photoelectric properties and sustainable miniaturiza-
tion capabilities have been leveraged to achieve visual sig-
nal
preprocessing
and
learning.28,29
Although
much
progress has been made, there is considerable space for
improvement in the stability and multiple memory states
of artificial vision devices.15,16 Fortunately, ferroelectric
materials exhibit controllable and reversible polarization
properties, making them great prospects in neuromorphic
memory devices, and the ferroelectric memristors are
promising candidates for new semiconducting memory
thanks to their simple structure, low operating power con-
sumption, high endurance, and multiple ferroelectric
domain states.30–34 The heterostructural memristors com-
bining 2D narrow bandgap materials with ferroelectric
materials offer a feasible pathway for a single device to
realize reservoir neuromorphic visual sensor applications
to mimic human retinal functions,35–40 which is attributed
to the modulation of carrier concentration and photoelec-
tric characteristics achieved by ferroelectric polarization
reversal using electrical and optical signals.41–43 Therefore,
2D/ferroelectric photoelectric synapses may provide a pro-
spective approach to construct a high-performance in-
sensor RC system integrating sensing-memory-computing
functions to implement face and fingerprint recognition.

In this study, we implemented an in-sensor RC
system constructed with MoTe2/BaTiO3 (BTO) optical syn-
apses to imitate the human vision system for high-
accuracy face and fingerprint recognition. Under light
stimulation, the device achieved low energy consumption
of 41.2 pJ, long retention time of 3  104 s, high endur-
ance of 104 switching cycles, multi-wavelength optical
response of 450/520/650 nm, 290 distinct current states,
and synaptic plasticity, including paired pulse facilitation
(PPF), short-term plasticity (STP), long-term plasticity
(LTP), long-term potentiation, and long-term depression.
Learning-forgetting-relearning, refractory period, Pavlov-
ian conditioning, “AND” “OR” logic functions were suc-
cessfully
emulated.
In
addition,
the
device
was
demonstrated to simulate sunburned eye simulation and
image memory functions using light intensity-dependent
optical sensing and multilevel optical storage properties.
These attributes allowed the MoTe2/BTO optical synapses
to
become
an
abundant
in-sensor
reservoir,
which
projected complicated input signals into high-dimensional
output representations. Therefore, the optical synapses-
based RC system demonstrated the input, projecting, char-
acterization, training, and recognition of face and finger-
print images, achieving the face recognition accuracy of
91.73% and the fingerprint recognition accuracy of 97.50%
under the 40% Gaussian noise environment with high
robustness to noise. The work continues to perform well
in hardware validation. These results suggest that the
neuromorphic vision system with MoTe2/BTO optical
memristors can play a potentially critical role in financial
services and communications applications.

unstructured realistic issues at a low energy consumption.44
The RC system is functionally divided into two sections, as
shown in the dashed box of Figure 1A. In the first section,
the
reservoir
layer
can
transform
the
input
signal
nonlinearly because it changes dynamically with the input
signal and also correlated with the history state.45 In the
second section, the readout layer is able to train the connec-
tion weights in a linearly weighted combination way,
enabling it simple to obtain the desired result. Since only
the connection weights of the output layer are changed,
rather than the reservoir layer, the system cuts down the
training
cost
dramatically.

Characterization and optical
synaptic characteristics of the MoTe2/BTO
sensor
Figure 2A shows the high-resolution transmission elec-
tron microscope (TEM) image with layered crystal
structure. The interlayer distance of 0.71 nm corresponds
to the (002) plane.51 It is clear from the inset that the Mo
atoms in the middle layer are sandwiched between the S
atoms in the two side layers. The selected area electron
diffraction (SAED) image confirms the 2H phase of
MoTe2 crystalline structure with hexagonally symmetric
diffraction spots, as shown in Figure 2B. Figure 2C fur-
ther validates the elemental distribution and composition
of the MoTe2 through the energy dispersive x-ray spec-
troscopy (EDS) mapping. The EDS spectrum shows the
atomic percentages of the elements Mo and Te are 32.7%
and 67.3%, respectively, which is very close to 1:2
(Figure S2). These microstructural characterizations indi-
cate the high-quality MoTe2 crystals. Figure 2D shows
the epitaxial crystalline states with atomic resolution of
BTO. Figure 2E also shows the perfect Fast Fourier
Transform (FFT) image. As shown in Figure 2F, the XPS
peaks at 228.01 and 231.19 eV correspond to the binding
energies of Mo 3d5/2 spectra and 3d3/2, respectively.
Figure 2G shows the Te 3d5/2 core level appears at 572.74
and Te 3d3/2 at 586.36 eV. These existing spectra are char-
acteristic peaks of the 2H phase in MoTe2.52,53 Figure S3
confirms good ferroelectricity of the BTO film. Under the
applied ±5 V voltage, the saturated polarization can
reach 43 μC/cm2. The piezoresponse force microscopy
(PFM) measurements show 180 phase reversal and sym-
metric hysteresis lines. The optical synaptic function of
MoTe2/BTO films can be explained by a recently pro-
posed
theory
considering
the
interplay
between
photogenerated
charges
in
MoTe2
and
polarization
charges in BTO. This is consistent with the recent works
using the 2D/ferroelectric structures.41,42 Due to the
MoTe2/BTO/LSMO
heterojunction
being
essentially
asymmetric, the downward built-in electric field will exist
in the heterostructure. The ratio of different ferroelectric
domain reversal directions in the BTO can also lead to
multiple current states.43 The dynamics of the light-
induced conductance change is analyzed in detail in the
Supporting Information: Note.54
To validate the temporal dynamics in the device, tran-
sient optical response measurements of the synaptic
device were carried out by applying a series of light
pulses (450 nm, 70 mW/cm2). As shown in Figure 2H,
two consecutive light pulse stimulations induce a gradual
current increase in the device, and the increment is
inversely correlated with the pulse interval. This is a typi-
cal PPF phenomenon in biology and an important feature
of STP. The PPF index has decreased from a maximum of
120% obtained at the time of 0.5 s to 103% at the time of
5 s. The postsynaptic current of the device corresponds to
the conductance value of the device or the neural synap-
tic connection strength.55 By adjusting the stimulus level,
the synapse plasticity can be regulated. Continuous light

Figure S5 shows five stable cycles of long-term potentia-
tion and depression. Both the long-term potentiation and
depression play important roles in the implementation of
memory and learning functions of ANNs. Relying on the
brain's strong synaptic plasticity, humans can learn new
knowledge and adapt to environmental changes through
continuous practice (Figure S6). As shown in Figures 2L
and S7, after a learning process of 64 s, the synaptic cur-
rent increased from 0.05 to 2.01, followed by a forgetting
process of 41 s, and the synaptic current consequently
decreased to 0.35. After a second shorter learning period
(39 s), the synaptic current returned to 2.00. The subse-
quent forgetting process was slower than the first, indi-
cating an enhanced level of memory in the device. This
completely
simulates
the
process
of
learning-
forgetting-relearning in the human brain.13 In addition,
the refractory period, Pavlovian conditioning, “AND,”
“OR” logic functions were successfully simulated (see
Figures S8–S10 for detailed explanation). According to
the formula of E = S  P  T, where S is the area of the
device, P is the power density of the optical spike with
the duration of T. So the single power consumption of
the optical device is 41.2 pJ (Figure S11). It can be
observed that the device has significant advantages in
terms of power consumption and is comparable with that
of the biological synapse. The synaptic current of the
device can be effectively modulated by light irradiation
(applying light, 450 nm, 10/20/50/70 mW/cm2), and well
maintained for 3  104 s after removing the light source
(Figure S12). This greatly increases the possibility of the
application of the long retention time states in multi-level
storage and computing. The reliability of the device is
investigated
by
using
potentiation
(applying
light,
450 nm, from bottom to top: 10/20/50/70 mW/cm2) and
depression (removing the light source) to switch the

rent
over
time
under
multi-wavelength
light
(450/520/650 nm) is shown in Figure S14, revealing the
ability of the MoTe2/BTO device to absorb and respond
to visible light. And we compare the parameters of our
device with other similar devices, demonstrating that
our
device
significantly
outperforms
the
others

in the visual synapses.21,56 These provide a prerequisite
for the implementation of in-sensor RC computing that
mimics the human visual system.

Sunburned eye simulation and
image memory functions
Human eyes are susceptible to sunlight damage such as
stinging and blindness. Accordingly, an eye injury sen-
sory model for different sunburned levels is proposed.
Here, three different degrees of sunlight damage to the
eyes were simulated by varying the light pulse exposure
time, the interval between neighboring light pulses, and
the number of light pulse irradiations to measure the cur-
rent of the device. Figure 3A–C show severe eye damage
under strong sunlight exposure, mild damage under dis-
continuous sunlight exposure, and moderate damage
under multiple sunlight exposures, respectively. The
same light intensity was applied in the following mea-
surements
(450 nm,
70 mW/cm2).
As
shown
in
Figure 3D, with the increased light duration applied to
the device, the synaptic current increases, representing
increased eye damage. Notice that the threshold current
was set at 0.66 μA, with the excess representing the dam-
age severity. As shown in Figure 3E, it can be seen that
the Δsynaptic current induced by 1 s of light exposure is
0.68 μA, and the Δsynaptic current induced by 4 s of light
exposure increases to 1.34 μA. This reminds us to avoid
serious damage caused by prolonged exposure to sunlight
in our life. As shown in Figure 3F, the synaptic current
tended to decrease as the time interval between two adja-
cent light pulses increased. As shown in Figure 3G, it can
be seen that the Δsynaptic current induced at the light
interval of 1 s was 0.82 μA, and the Δsynaptic current
induced at the light interval of 4 s decreases to 0.64 μA.
Obviously, this reminds us to try to prolong the time
interval between adjacent sunlight exposures in our life
to mitigate the degree of damage, even for mild sunburn.
As shown in Figure 3H, the synaptic current increases as
the amount of light exposure increases. As shown in

generate the cat image. The relatively dim cat image in
Figure 4F corresponds to synaptic current of 5 light
pulses. Then, after 5 and 15 s of the forgetting process,
the image is gradually faded. When observed again after
25 s, the blurred image outline is observed, indicating
that 5 training sessions have little effect on the memory
features of the image. Under increased light pulses
(15 pulses), the image sharpness and learning process
become enhanced. After forgetting for 5, 15, and 25 s, a
clear image can still be observed (Figure 4G). When the

would be slower when experiencing the same forgetting

is
very
similar
to
the

and

2.4
|
Nonlinear mapping of 4-bit inputs
and face recognition with the in-sensor RC
system
Traditional
feedforward
neural
networks
including
ANN and CNN face serious problems of gradient explo-
sion as well as gradient vanishing during training
period. Notably, when dealing with data intensive tasks
with higher computing power requirements, the num-
ber of neurons and parameters in the network increase
rapidly, which makes the processing efficiency insuffi-
cient
to
handle.
Recent
studies
have
shown
that
memristor-based RC computing effectively addresses
these challenges due to its simplicity, high efficiency,
and low computational cost advantages.57–60 However,
transforming and encoding the image in the form of
electrical pulses is not favorable for energy conserva-
tion.29 Here we employ optical signals to directly trigger
the nonlinear and spatio-temporally correlated synaptic
current response of the memristor to simulate short-
term memory in RC system. In the practical application
of optical information acquisition, due to the quantum
nature of light, speckle noise can be caused.61 In addi-
tion, the electronic circuit device will produce thermal
noise due to temperature, and thermal noise will cause
random fluctuations in the output electrical signal,
resulting in further noise in the image and decrease in
recognition accuracy. We add Gaussian noise with dif-
ferent levels to the image to simulate the blur caused
by speckle noise and thermal noise. So we construct
the in-sensor RC system based on MoTe2/BTO optical
synapses for biometric identification. The performance
of the system is verified by using the Yale face recogni-
tion dataset with different noise levels.62 Firstly, the
noisy face image of size 64  64 is scaled and binarized
to a binary image of 10  4, meanwhile 10 devices are
used to construct the reservoir layer, as shown in
Figure 5A. In detail, light pulses encoded by the scaled
image are applied on the devices, and the input state u
(t) of the reservoir is formed with transient inputs from
all the synapses at time t. With the dynamic evolution
of the state x(t) inside the reservoir layer, the input u(t)
can be successfully projected to the high-dimensional
feature space y(t). The high-dimensional feature space y
(t) is then processed as a new input to the following
network. By encoding the spatial information as a time
series u(t), the size of the network used for image
processing is significantly reduced. In addition, the out-
put layer use dropout neurons. Here, the dropout prob-
ability P is set to 0.3. Dropout will randomly select
neurons to drop during training, which can reduce the
overfitting of the model to the training data, improve
the model's generalization ability to new data, and
increase the robustness of the model. Because the net-
work is not overly dependent on any particular neuron,
different combinations of subnetworks are used several
times when training.
As shown in Figure 5B, as the noise level increases,
the raw images gradually become blurred, which truly
simulates the noise situation in real life. Moreover, the
noise
points
of
the
scaled
images
also
increase.
The Figures S15 and S16 show more of the original and
scaled images with different noise levels. The optical

and the good results are shown in Figure 5D. It can be
seen that the individual states of the device are essen-
tially in 16 separable states at 4.8 s after four pulses, so
the synaptic current at the moment of 4.8 s is selected.
The synaptic current is measured five times to assure

CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we constructed an in-sensor RC system
composed of a photo-synapse reservoir layer and a read-
out layer for biometric recognition, including faces and
fingerprints information. It is found that the optical syn-
apse shows low energy consumption of 41.2 pJ, a long
retention time of 3  104 s, high endurance of 104
switching cycles, a multi-wavelength optical response of
450/520/650 nm, a high number of states (290 states) and
successfully simulates PPF, STP, LTP, long-term potentia-
tion,
long-term
depression,
learning-forgetting-
relearning, refractory period, Pavlovian conditioning,
“AND” “OR” logic functions. The sunburned eye simula-
tion and image storage capabilities were demonstrated.
These excellent neuromorphic features can be used as
reservoir inputs, which can be projected nonlinearly to
the high-dimensional outputs in the feature region. Then,
a simple readout network responsible for training is able
to achieve efficient recognition and computing. Under
the
40%
Gaussian
noise
environment,
this
system
achieves high recognition accuracy of 91.73% for face rec-
ognition after 200 training epochs and 97.5% for finger-
print recognition within 100 training epochs, which is
24.49% higher than ANN in accuracy and reduced by
99.98% in training parameters number. The in-sensor RC
system based on MoTe2/BTO optical synapses provides a
reference for efficient authentication and information
security.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
4.1
|
Device fabrication
To prepare the Pd/MoTe2/BTO/LSMO/STO device, the
LSMO bottom electrode film and the BTO ferroelectric
film were firstly grown sequentially on a single-crystal
STO substrate using pulsed laser deposition. The STO
substrate was cleaned in deionized water with ultrasonic
waves for 5 min and then dried with pure nitrogen. The
vacuum in the chamber was kept below 2  104 Pa
before film deposition. During the deposition of LSMO
and BTO films, the deposition temperature was 750C
and the deposition gas (oxygen) pressure was 26 and
1 Pa, respectively. The distance between the sample and
the target was kept at 7 cm, and the rotational speed of
the sample and the target was kept at 5/s with the laser
frequency of 5 Hz. After the deposition, the devices were
kept in situ and annealed for 10 min, then cooled under
an oxygen pressure atmosphere of 1  103 Pa. The pre-
pared BTO/LSMO/STO films were placed on a suction
cup in the middle of the spin coater with a rotational
speed of 1200 rpm and a rotation time of 40 s. The 20 μL
of MoTe2 solution was spin-coated on the surface of the
BTO/LSMO/STO films. Once the spin coating was com-
pleted, the substrate was moved to a vacuum drying oven
and the temperature was set to 40C. The substrate was
allowed to dry for 30 min and the above steps were
repeated
again.

Abstract: The artificial intelligence era has witnessed a surge of demand in detection and recognition of biometric information, with applications from financial services to information security. However, the physical separation of sensing, memory, and computational units in traditional biometric systems introduces severe decision latency and operational power consumption. Herein, an in-sensor res- ervoir computing (RC) system based on MoTe2/BaTiO3 optical synapses is pro- posed to detect and recognize the faces and fingerprints information. In optical operation mode, the device exhibits low energy consumption of 41.2 pJ, long retention time of 3  104 s, high endurance of 104 switching cycles, and multifunctional sensing-memory-computing visual simulations. The light intensity-dependent optical sensing and multilevel optical storage properties are exploited to achieve sunburned eye simulation and image memory func- tions. These nonlinear, multi-state, short-term storage, and long-term memory characteristics make MoTe2/BaTiO3 optical synapses a suitable reservoir layer and readout layer, with short-term properties to project complicated input fea- tures into high-dimensional output features, and long-term properties to be used as a readout layer, thus further building an in-sensor RC system for face and fingerprint recognition. Under the 40% Gaussian noise environment, the system achieves 91.73% recognition accuracy for face and 97.50% for finger- print images, and experimental verification is carried out, which shows poten- tial in practical applications. These results provide a strategy for constructing a high-performance in-sensor RC system for high-accuracy biometric identification. Zhenqiang Guo and Gongjie Liu contributed equally to this study.
